objectives: Say who the first peoples and kingdoms of Cameroon were and how Cameroon got its name.
Describe the German period and the division between Britain and France.
Put the main events in order on a timeline.
reviewNotes: Facts about Cameroon are limited to well-established, neutral points; dates and names to be checked by a teacher against the official textbook.
Dates (1472, 1884, 1916) are those commonly given in school textbooks; 1472 is approximate. Mention of resistance and forced labour is deliberately brief; textbook wording to be checked.
The slave trade era is not covered.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Early times and the name Cameroon
blocks.md: Many peoples have lived in the land of Cameroon for a very long time, for example forest peoples such as the Baka, farming peoples and the peoples of the Grassfields, with kingdoms and chiefdoms such as the **Bamum** in the West and the **Duala** chiefs on the coast. In about **1472** Portuguese sailors arrived at the River Wouri and called it the *river of prawns* (*Rio dos Camarões*). The name **Cameroon** comes from this.

blocks.caption: Three important dates before independence.
blocks.alt: A timeline from 1450 to 1930 with three events: Portuguese arrive about 1472, German protectorate 1884, Britain and France take over in 1916.

blocks.title: German rule
blocks.md: In **1884** the Duala chiefs signed treaties with Germany, and the country became a German **protectorate** called *Kamerun*. The Germans built roads, railways and plantations. Many Cameroonians were made to work for them, and some people resisted. German rule lasted until the First World War.

blocks.title: Britain and France
blocks.md: In the First World War, British and French forces took Kamerun. By **1916** the Germans had left. The country was **divided** between **Britain** (a smaller part in the west, the British Cameroons) and **France** (a larger part, French Cameroun). The League of Nations gave them **mandates** to rule, and after 1945 the United Nations gave them **trusteeship**. This is why Cameroon has two official languages today.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Saying that Cameroon was always one country: it was divided in 1916.
- Mixing up the dates: 1472 (Portuguese), 1884 (German protectorate), 1916 (Britain and France).
- Thinking that the Portuguese ruled Cameroon: they only traded on the coast.
- Giving opinions as facts; in history we use sources and dates.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: How did Cameroon get its name?
steps: About 1472 Portuguese sailors reached the River Wouri.
They found many prawns and named it the river of prawns, Rio dos Camarões. Later the name became Cameroon.
blocks.answer: From Rio dos Camarões, the Portuguese name for the River Wouri (the river of prawns).

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: How many years passed between the German treaties (1884) and the division between Britain and France (1916)?

objectives: Explain how French Cameroun and the British Cameroons became independent.
Say what 20 May, 11 February and 1 October celebrate.
reviewNotes: Facts about Cameroon are limited to well-established, neutral points; dates and names to be checked by a teacher against the official textbook.

Dates are standard facts (1 Jan 1960, 11 Feb 1961, 1 Oct 1961, 20 May 1972, name change 1984, Ahidjo to 1982, Biya from 1982); the political situation after 1990 and debates about the 1961 union are deliberately NOT covered. Wording about 1 October should be checked against the textbook (it is not celebrated in the same way everywhere).
Neutral tone required: a teacher should check that no opinion has entered.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Independence
blocks.md: French Cameroun became **independent** on **1 January 1960**, with **Ahmadou Ahidjo** as its first president. **Nigeria** became independent on 1 October 1960. The British Cameroons (Northern and Southern) were still under British trusteeship, so the United Nations arranged a **plebiscite** (a vote of the people) there.

blocks.caption: Independence, reunification and the United Republic.
blocks.alt: A timeline arrow with three dates: 1960, French Cameroun becomes independent; 1961, Southern Cameroons joins and a federation is formed; 1972, the United Republic of Cameroon on 20 May.

blocks.title: The 1961 plebiscite
blocks.md: On **11 February 1961** the people of the British Cameroons voted. **Northern Cameroons** chose to join **Nigeria**. **Southern Cameroons** chose to join the Republic of **Cameroon**. On **1 October 1961** Southern Cameroons joined, and the country became the **Federal Republic of Cameroon**, with two federated states (East and West). This is called **reunification**.

blocks.title: Later changes and national days
blocks.md: On **20 May 1972** a referendum created the **United Republic of Cameroon**, one state instead of two federated states; in 1984 it was renamed the **Republic of Cameroon**. Ahidjo was president until 1982, and **Paul Biya** has been president since 1982. National days: **11 February** (Youth Day), **20 May** (National Day) and **1 October** (reunification of the two Cameroons, celebrated in some places).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Mixing 1960 (independence of French Cameroun) and 1961 (joining of Southern Cameroons).
- Saying that all the British Cameroons joined Cameroon: the Northern part chose Nigeria.
- Mixing 11 February (Youth Day) and 20 May (National Day).
- Giving opinions about politics: in this subject we learn the facts and dates.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: How many years passed from independence (1960) to the United Republic (1972)?

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: What did the people of the Southern Cameroons decide in the 1961 plebiscite?
steps: They chose to join the Republic of Cameroon, while Northern Cameroons chose Nigeria.
blocks.answer: They chose to join the Republic of Cameroon.
